items.title: Ted Piltzecker interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 10, 2019
items.q: the same principles apply negotiating a jazz solo that apply to Palestrina or James Brown or Henry Moore or Becket.

ctx.x: The question of out and in, you played some things this morning, I should sort of describe, we were doing some things for the students under the auspices of our jazz professor Michael Woods. And I have this thing I do when someone plays something that I think is highly hip or unexpected or, in short, something I never would have thought of. And I find myself raising my eyebrows or, like turning my head. And you made me do that four or five times. And I just wanted to compliment you on the way you took things sort…

I think like any improviser it’s not on a conscious level. Things become habitual. You’re — manipulating parameters becomes habitual. You don’t think about the notes in a chord or a scale or which finger to push down to play when you improvise. But you think about the concept and the idea. But on the broader sense, not just playing an instrument and negotiating the changes, on a broader sense the same thing can happen in composition where you make it a habit of thinking consciously at first about texture, about…

tempo, because you’ve got it. The same thing can happen compositionally when you start, you know you almost run through this checklist in a nanosecond about what’s at play right now in terms of composition, and then make decisions that are appropriate. That’s — I’d like to say that I aspire toward that. Sometimes it happens you know, but that I think is starting now. I think about myself as not an instrumentalist so much as just as a musician. And the same principles — that’s the cool thing — the same principles…
